hypothesis: In some types of non-Alzheimer's, non-aged human brain cells, APOE4 undergoes increased aggregation in the endo-lysosome compared with APOE3.

rows.Finding description: After purification, apoE4M lacking residues 1–23 aggregated almost instantaneously, whereas the corresponding apoE3M construct required several hours.
rows.Finding quote: Interestingly, while the aggregation of ApoE4M-AP occurred almost instantaneously, it took several hours to observe the aggregation of ApoE3M-AP.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3M-AP -> apoE4M-AP) -> (faster apoE aggregation)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human apoE3M and apoE4M, each carrying F257A/W264R/V269A/L279Q/V287E and deletion of residues 1–23. Aggregation observed following size-exclusion purification. This is an engineered, lipid-free protein system without endo-lysosomes.
rows.Data location: Results accompanying Fig. 3G: “Interestingly, while the aggregation of ApoE4M-AP occurred almost instantaneously, it took several hours to observe the aggregation of ApoE3M-AP.”

rows.Finding description: Adding SPA reduced apoE4 aggregation toward the apoE3 level during static light scattering at 37 °C, with three replicates.
rows.Finding quote: The signal from light scattering decreased in the presence of both SPA (Fig. 5A) and tramiprosate (Supplementary Fig. 10), suggesting the reduction of ApoE4 aggregation.
rows.Finding summary: (SPA added to apoE4) -> (reduced apoE aggregation)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human wild-type apoE4 at approximately 10 µM, with 20 mM SPA, a 2000-fold molar excess. Static light scattering at 266 nm over 15 hours in Tris buffer at 37 °C and pH 7.4; apoE3 served as a comparator.

rows.Finding description: Truncated apoE4M aggregated almost instantaneously, while four additional interface alanine substitutions prevented aggregation; the photographed AP/AS comparison was reproduced in at least two independent experiments.
rows.Finding quote: Interestingly, while the aggregation of ApoE4M-AP occurred almost instantaneously, it took several hours to observe the aggregation of ApoE3M-AP. Subsequent transmission electron microscopy (TEM) analysis of these aggregates revealed fibril-like morphology in both cases (Fig. 3H). Conversely, no aggregation was observed for ApoE3M-AS and ApoE4M-AS.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE4M-AP -> apoE4M-AS interface mutations) -> (suppressed apoE aggregation)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant ApoE3M and ApoE4M truncation constructs. The Results identify both isoforms for the AP aggregation and AS suppression observations. Fig. 3G labels the photographed samples generically as ApoEM-AP and ApoEM-AS.

rows.Finding description: Transmission electron microscopy found fibril-like apoE aggregates in both truncated apoE3M and apoE4M preparations, without reporting a quantitative between-isoform difference in fibril burden.
rows.Finding quote: Subsequent transmission electron microscopy (TEM) analysis of these aggregates revealed fibril-like morphology in both cases (Fig. 3H).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3M-AP -> apoE4M-AP) -> (fibril-like aggregates present in both)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human apoE3M-AP and apoE4M-AP, carrying five monomerizing substitutions and deletion of residues 1–23. Negative-stain TEM using approximately 0.4 mg/ml protein and 2% ammonium molybdate. Legend specifically identifies the pictured apoE3M-AP fibrils; Results reports both isoforms.

rows.Finding description: Adaptive simulations showed apoE3 dimer dissociation after approximately 2.5 µs of cumulative sampling, whereas apoE4 did not dissociate even after approximately 10 µs.
rows.Finding quote: While the ApoE3 dimeric unit dissociated after ~ 2.5 µs, the dissociation of the ApoE4 dimeric unit did not occur even after ~ 10 µs.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (greater simulated persistence of the N-terminal dimer)
rows.Experimental system: Adaptive molecular dynamics of human apoE N-terminal dimers initialized from apoE3 structure 1BZ4 and apoE4 structure 8AX9. Simulations used 310 K, pH 7.4 protonation and 0.1 M salt. Reported times are cumulative adaptive sampling, not measured cellular lifetimes.

rows.Finding description: The simulated apoE4 dimer had a more favorable mean electrostatic interaction energy, −396 kcal/mol, than apoE3, −338 kcal/mol, a 1.17-fold greater magnitude.
rows.Finding quote: We also found significantly stronger binding energy in the dimeric unit of ApoE4 than in ApoE3, explaining its resilience to dissociation. These interactions were formed primarily by electrostatic contacts (Supplementary Tables 8 and Supplementary Note 1).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (stronger simulated electrostatic dimer association)
rows.Experimental system: Human apoE N-terminal dimer adaptive molecular dynamics without SPA. Linear interaction energies calculated over the first 500 ns of concatenated trajectories while dimers remained associated; 310 K, pH 7.4 protonation and 0.1 M salt.
rows.Data location: Supplementary Table 8, ApoE3 and ApoE4 Eelec rows

rows.Finding description: Proteolytic mapping lacked N-terminal peptides around residues 31–50 for wild-type apoE3 and 44–52 for wild-type apoE4, indicating interface protection in both with different coverage boundaries.
rows.Finding quote: Based on LC-MS/MS bottom-up proteomics analysis of both ApoEWT and ApoEM, we found that wild-type ApoE3 and ApoE4 isoforms lack peptides in NTD corresponding to residues ~ 31–50 and 44–52, respectively (Fig. 4A, CTD in Supplementary Fig. 7).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3WT -> apoE4WT) -> (different protease-inaccessible regions at the self-association interface)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human wild-type apoE3 and apoE4, compared with monomerizing-mutant proteins, using proteolysis and LC-MS/MS peptide mapping. Missing coverage was interpreted as protection in oligomeric protein, without direct aggregate quantification or endo-lysosomal localization.

rows.Finding description: Simulations showed partial unfolding at H3 residues 89–94 in apoE3 but not apoE4, whereas apoE4 lost helical content at residues 120–124 near Q123.
rows.Finding quote: The results showed partial unfolding at the N-terminus of the H3 helix (residues 89–94) in the case of ApoE3, while no change was observed in ApoE4. Conversely, we observed a significant decrease in α-helical content at the end of the H3 helix (residues 120–124) in ApoE4.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3M -> apoE4M) -> (less N-terminal but greater C-terminal H3 unfolding)
rows.Experimental system: Adaptive simulations of full-length human apoE3M and apoE4M, twenty microseconds cumulative sampling per system at 310 K. Residue-level helical content calculated using DSSP. Misfolding-related structural readout, without endo-lysosomal localization.

rows.Finding description: Crystal-structure analysis found T-shaped packing in 6 of 8 apoE3 structures and V-shaped packing in 5 of 7 apoE4 structures, supporting an isoform-associated difference in self-association geometry.
rows.Finding quote: A comparison of previously solved ApoE structures revealed that ApoE2 and ApoE3 prefer T-shaped packing, as 2 out of 2 ApoE2 structures and 6 out of 8 ApoE3 structures display T-shaped packing. On the other hand, 5 of the 7 ApoE4 structures have V-shaped packing, indicating an ApoE4 preference for this packing pattern.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (greater preference for V-shaped N-terminal self-association)
rows.Experimental system: Comparative crystallographic analysis of human apoE N-terminal domains, combining existing structures with four newly determined apoE4 structures. New crystals arose from recombinant MBP-apoE4M preparations but resolved approximately residues 22–165. Crystal packing is a proposed aggregation surrogate; no brain cells, acidic compartment or endo-lysosomal localization was tested.

rows.Finding description: The apoE4-preferred V-shaped dimer had an approximately 75° interchain angle, compared with approximately 100° for the apoE3-preferred T-shaped dimer, a 25° difference.
rows.Finding quote: While the angle between chains A and B in the T-shaped dimeric unit was ~ 100°, the corresponding angle in the V-shaped dimeric unit was significantly smaller ~ 75°. This ~ 25° angle difference between T-shaped and V-shaped packing was retained in both the orthorhombic and trigonal space groups.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (smaller angle between self-associating N-terminal domains)
rows.Experimental system: Human apoE N-terminal crystal structures; interchain angles derived from principal axes of inertia. Comparison concerns crystal-associated dimers, without cellular or endo-lysosomal aggregation measurements.

rows.Finding description: Compared with apoE3-like T-shaped structures, apoE4 C112R structures formed an R112–E109 salt bridge, lost the R61–E109 interaction and repositioned Q123 toward the proposed aggregation-prone geometry.
rows.Finding quote: The C112R substitution in ApoE4 (Fig. 1C and Supplementary Fig. 2) led to the formation of a new salt bridge between R112 and E109 and the repositioning of R61. Consequently, the helix H2-H3 interaction between R61 and E109 observed in the T-shaped packing was abolished, and the four-helix bundle was destabilized. The “domino-like” effect of the C112R mutation was further exacerbated through the H3 helix up towards Q123, which directly influenced a tilt between chains A and B. The side-chain of Q123 was oriented upwards in the T-shaped packing, while it was rotated downwards in the V-shaped packing.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 C112 -> apoE4 R112) -> (altered intradomain contacts and destabilized four-helix bundle)
rows.Experimental system: Comparative analysis of recombinant human apoE N-terminal crystal structures. The proposed domino mechanism links local structural differences to self-association; aggregation inside cells was not measured.

rows.Finding description: ApoE4 and apoE3 retained the same principal self-association interface, but apoE4 gained a D153–Q46 interaction and displayed a different W34 orientation.
rows.Finding quote: Despite a different tilt in T-shaped and V-shaped dimeric units, the main self-association interface formed by chains A and B remained the same in all ApoE isoforms (Fig. 1D). The key interacting residues that held the two chains together were R38 (H1) and R145 (H4) from chain A and E45 and E49 located in helix 1’ (H1’) of chain B. Additionally, a new specific interaction in ApoE4 was formed between D153 from chain A and Q46 from chain B as both chains were tilted in the ApoE4 structure. Moreover, E45 which interacts with R38 and R145, moved to the center of the “self-association interface”, causing a re-orientation of the W34 side chain upwards.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (additional contact within a shared self-association interface)
rows.Experimental system: Human apoE N-terminal crystal dimers, comparing apoE3-preferred T-shaped and apoE4-preferred V-shaped interfaces. No cellular compartment or aggregation amount was measured.

rows.Finding description: Wild-type apoE4 and apoE3 showed different hydrogen-deuterium uptake around residue 112 and in H3, H4 and the C-terminal domain, indicating isoform-dependent conformation and solvent accessibility.
rows.Finding quote: The main differences between wild-type ApoE3 and ApoE4 isoforms in HDX-MS analysis were the deuterium uptakes (Fig. 4B and Supplementary Fig. 8) observed around position 112, including helix H3 (residues 79–123) and helix H4 (residues 134–136). Moreover, some differences were observed for the CTD, suggesting that C112R substitution has a long-range impact on the entire ApoE molecule and its tetramerization.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3WT -> apoE4WT) -> (altered solvent accessibility in aggregation-associated protein regions)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human wild-type apoE3 and apoE4; HDX-MS at room temperature in Tris/NaCl buffer, D2O buffer pHread 7.1. Exchange measured at 60, 120 and 600 seconds; main figure shows 60 seconds. No cellular or endo-lysosomal assay.

rows.Finding description: Simulated apoE4M H3 was approximately 7° less straight than apoE3M H3 and had a broader, skewed bending-angle distribution.
rows.Finding quote: We found that the H3 helix was ~ 7° straighter in ApoE3M than in ApoE4M. Moreover, ApoE4M showed a more spread and skewed distribution.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3M -> apoE4M) -> (increased H3 bending)
rows.Experimental system: Full-length human apoE3M and apoE4M adaptive molecular dynamics, twenty microseconds cumulative sampling per system at 310 K. H3 bending measured using the Cα atoms of residues 95, 106 and 117, with 180° representing an unbent helix. No cells or aggregates measured.

rows.Finding description: Both apoE3M and apoE4M were characterized as monomerized, rather than showing greater apoE4 oligomerization; no statistical between-isoform difference was reported.
rows.Finding quote: Moreover, we observed that the five mutations previously introduced into the ApoE code to monomerize both isoforms (ApoEM) simultaneously inhibit their aggregation (Supplementary Figs. 5 and 6).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3M -> apoE4M) -> (shared monomerized state)
rows.Experimental system: Purified recombinant human apoE3M and apoE4M carrying F257A/W264R/V269A/L279Q/V287E. Sedimentation velocity analytical ultracentrifugation at 0.8 mg/ml, 20 °C and 50,000 rpm, analyzed by continuous c(s) distributions. The supplied figure image is unavailable.

rows.Finding description: The simulated apoE4 dimer had mean van der Waals interaction energy of −41 kcal/mol versus −37 kcal/mol for apoE3, a 1.11-fold greater magnitude.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (slightly stronger simulated van der Waals dimer association)
rows.Experimental system: Human apoE N-terminal dimers without SPA; linear interaction energies from the first 500 ns of associated, concatenated adaptive MD trajectories at 310 K and pH 7.4 protonation.
rows.Data location: Supplementary Table 8, ApoE3 and ApoE4 EvdW rows

rows.Finding description: With SPA, the simulated apoE4 dimer retained a more favorable mean electrostatic interaction energy, −322 kcal/mol, than apoE3, −250 kcal/mol, a 1.29-fold greater magnitude.
rows.Finding quote: ApoE3+ SPA Eelec = -250 ± 69 EvdW = -39 ± 7 R145, R38, R142, R32, D35 E49, E45, E50 ApoE4+ SPA Eelec = -322 ± 73
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 + SPA -> apoE4 + SPA) -> (stronger simulated electrostatic dimer association)
rows.Experimental system: Human apoE N-terminal dimer adaptive MD with SPA; energies computed during the first 500 ns of concatenated associated trajectories. Simulations at 310 K, pH 7.4 protonation and 0.1 M salt.
rows.Data location: Supplementary Table 8, ApoE3+SPA and ApoE4+SPA Eelec rows

rows.Finding description: In simulations, the dominant W34 side-chain population was around χ1 = 180° in apoE3M and around χ1 = 300° in apoE4M.
rows.Finding quote: We found that ApoE3M displayed a majority of its population around χ1 = 180° while ApoE4M was mostly around χ1 = 300°.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3M -> apoE4M) -> (different W34 conformation at the self-association interface)
rows.Experimental system: Adaptive molecular dynamics of full-length human apoE3M and homology-modeled apoE4M, with five C-terminal monomerizing mutations. Twenty microseconds cumulative sampling per system at 310 K and pH 7.4 protonation; W34 χ1 distributions measured. Structural surrogate, not an aggregate measurement.

hypothesis: In some types of non-Alzheimer's, non-aged human brain cells, for example astrocytes, APOE4 causes impaired ARF6-related recycling of receptors between the cell surface and the endosome, compared with APOE3.

rows.Finding description: Confocal imaging of human SH-SY5Y neuronal cells expressing IR-GFP showed greater colocalization with transferrin-positive endosomes after apoE4 than apoE3 treatment without insulin (nearly 20% with apoE4); insulin increased colocalization in apoE3-treated cells but produced no significant difference in apoE4-treated cells, with three independent experiments reported.
rows.Finding quote: In the absence of insulin, we found that nearly 20% of IR-GFP co-localized with transferrin in the endosomal compartment in apoE4-treated cells whereas less co-localization was observed in apoE3-treated cells (Figures 6A and 6D). Insulin induced IR internalization which increased the co-localization of IR-GFP with transferrin in apoE3-treated cells, but not in apoE4-treated cells (Figures 6A and 6D).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (greater IR-GFP localization in transferrin-positive endosomes without insulin; no change in colocalization upon insulin stimulation with apoE4)
rows.Experimental system: Human SH-SY5Y neuronal cell line, source unspecified, transfected with human IR-GFP plasmid (Addgene #22286); 24 hours after transfection, treated overnight with 100 nM recombinant apoE3 or apoE4, with or without 100 nM insulin during the final 30 minutes; Alexa Fluor 568-labeled human transferrin (20 μg/ml) added one hour before fixation; confocal fluorescence microscopy after 4% PFA fixation.

rows.Finding description: Across three independent experiments, human SH-SY5Y cells expressing IR-GFP and treated overnight with apoE4 versus apoE3 showed increased intracellular receptor fractions without insulin (nearly 40% versus 15%), while insulin increased this fraction with apoE3 but produced no significant difference with apoE4.
rows.Finding quote: In the absence of insulin, the majority of the IR-GFP was localized to the cell membrane with only 15% of the receptor localized intracellularly in apoE3-treated cells (Figures 6A–C). Interestingly, nearly 40% of IR-GFP was localized in the intracellular compartment in apoE4-treated cells (Figures 6A–C), consistent with our observation in which apoE4 reduced cell surface IR (Figures 5G–I). Importantly, insulin stimulation increased the percentage of intracellular IR-GFP in apoE3-treated, but not in apoE4-treated, cells (Figures 6A–C).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (higher intracellular IR-GFP fraction without insulin; no change in intracellular IR-GFP fraction after insulin in apoE4-treated cells)
rows.Experimental system: Human SH-SY5Y neuronal cells transfected with human IR-GFP plasmid (Addgene #22286) using Lipofectamine 3000; 24 hours after transfection, treated overnight with 100 nM recombinant apoE3 or apoE4, with or without 100 nM insulin for 30 minutes before fixation; confocal microscopy quantified intracellular IR-GFP as a fraction of total IR-GFP. Cell supplier and donor age were not stated; ARF6 activity and recycling kinetics were not measured in this panel.

rows.Finding description: In primary Apoe−/− mouse cortical neurons treated with recombinant apoE3 or apoE4, a cleavable-biotin trafficking assay showed significantly more intracellular biotinylated insulin receptor at 60 minutes with apoE4, although internalization plateaued at 30 minutes with both isoforms, suggesting delayed receptor recycling.
rows.Finding quote: The internalization of IR reached plateau at 30 minutes after treatment with either apoE3 or apoE4 (Figure S8A). After 60 minutes treatment with apoE3, the amount of internalized (biotinylated) IR was reduced, reflecting a membrane recycling of IR and subsequent biotin cleavage. Interestingly, apoE4-treated cells exhibited significantly more intracellular IR compared to those treated with apoE3 at 60 minutes, suggesting a delayed recycling of IR in the presence of apoE4 (Figure S8A).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (increased intracellular biotinylated insulin receptor at 60 minutes in primary mouse cortical neurons)
rows.Experimental system: Primary cortical neurons from embryonic day 16–18 Apoe−/− mice; treated with 100 nM recombinant apoE3 or apoE4 at 37°C, with internalization plateauing at 30 minutes and the comparison assessed at 60 minutes; cell-surface proteins labeled with cleavable sulfo-NHS-SS-biotin, remaining surface biotin removed with glutathione, and intracellular biotinylated insulin receptor quantified by streptavidin precipitation and Western blotting.

rows.Finding description: In three independent experiments, surface biotinylation and Western blotting of primary Apoe−/− mouse cortical neurons treated with apoE3, apoE4 or vehicle, with or without insulin, showed that apoE4 reduced surface insulin receptor without insulin and suppressed insulin-stimulated Akt signaling compared with apoE3.
rows.Finding quote: In the absence of insulin stimulation, we found that apoE4 but not apoE3 significantly reduced the amount of cell surface IR (Figures 5G, H).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (lower cell-surface insulin receptor without insulin and reduced insulin-stimulated Akt signaling in primary mouse cortical neurons)
rows.Experimental system: Primary cortical neurons from embryonic day 16–18 Apoe−/− mice; glia eliminated with Ara-C at DIV5; at DIV10, treated overnight with vehicle or recombinant apoE3 or apoE4 (100 nM), with or without insulin stimulation (100 nM, 30 minutes); cell-surface biotinylation followed by Western blotting for surface and total IR, p-Akt (Ser473), total Akt and β-actin.

rows.Finding description: Primary Apoe−/− mouse neurons treated with apoE4 versus apoE3 showed no significant difference in cell surface LRP1 levels measured by cell surface biotinylation.
rows.Finding quote: No significant differences were found in the levels of cell surface and total LRP1, NMDAR, AMPAR, and Na-K-ATPase after apoE3 and apoE4 treatments (Figures S7A, C–F, H–K).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (no change in cell surface LRP1 levels in primary Apoe−/− mouse neurons)
rows.Experimental system: Primary cortical neurons obtained from embryonic day 16–18 Apoe−/− mice; glia eliminated with Ara-C at DIV5. Cell surface biotinylation methods specify overnight treatment at DIV10 with 100 nM recombinant apoE, followed by surface protein isolation and Western blotting. Panel-specific treatment details could not be verified because the supplement was unavailable.

rows.Finding description: Cell-surface biotinylation in primary Apoe−/− mouse cortical neurons showed that insulin-induced insulin receptor internalization reached a plateau at 5 minutes without apoE, 15 minutes with apoE3, and 30 minutes with apoE4, with subsequent intracellular receptor levels declining without apoE or with apoE3 but showing no obvious decline with apoE4.
rows.Finding quote: Insulin induced rapid endocytosis of IR with the plateau appeared at 5 minutes and then steadily declined, reflecting membrane recycling of IR and subsequent biotin cleavage (Figure S9). In the presence of apoE3, the plateau of the curve shifted to 15 minutes and then started to decline (Figure S9). However, in the presence of apoE4, the internalization of IR did not approach plateau until 30 minutes and without obvious decline over time (Figure S9), indicating that apoE4 inhibited insulin-induced IR trafficking.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (delayed insulin-induced IR internalization and impaired subsequent recycling in primary mouse cortical neurons)
rows.Experimental system: Primary cortical neurons from embryonic day 16–18 Apoe−/− mice; surface proteins labeled with cleavable biotin at 4°C, followed by insulin (100 nM) without apoE or with recombinant apoE3 or apoE4 (100 nM) at 37°C over time; remaining surface biotin removed with glutathione, and intracellular biotinylated IR quantified by precipitation and Western blotting. ARF6 involvement was not measured.

rows.Finding description: Primary Apoe−/− mouse cortical neurons exposed to recombinant apoE4 versus apoE3 retained significantly more intracellular biotinylated insulin receptor at 30 and 60 minutes during recycling, indicating slower return to the cell surface; ARF6 was not measured.
rows.Finding quote: Intriguingly, significantly higher amount of intracellular IR was detected in apoE4-treated cells compared with cells treated with apoE3 at 30 minutes and 60 minutes, indicating that apoE4 impaired IR recycling (Figure S8B).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (impaired insulin receptor recycling to the cell surface in primary mouse cortical neurons)
rows.Experimental system: Primary cortical neurons from embryonic day 16–18 Apoe−/− mice; surface receptors labeled with cleavable biotin, followed by 100 nM recombinant apoE3 or apoE4 for 30 minutes at 37°C to permit internalization; apoE removed and recycling assessed at 30 and 60 minutes by glutathione cleavage of surface biotin, streptavidin precipitation, and Western blotting of residual intracellular insulin receptor.

rows.Finding description: In primary Apoe−/− mouse cortical neurons treated overnight with recombinant apoE3 or apoE4, insulin stimulation for 30 minutes caused a smaller decrease in surface-to-total insulin receptor after apoE4 treatment, with approximately 20% versus 50% internalization, respectively, across three independent experiments.
rows.Finding quote: Importantly, ~50% of the total IR was internalized in response to insulin in apoE3-treated cells, whereas only ~20% of IR was internalized in apoE4-treated cells upon insulin stimulation (Figure 5I).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (smaller insulin-induced decrease in surface-to-total insulin receptor in primary mouse cortical neurons)
rows.Experimental system: Primary cortical neurons from embryonic day 16–18 Apoe−/− mice; glia eliminated with Ara-C at DIV5; at DIV10, treated overnight with 100 nM recombinant apoE3 or apoE4, followed by 100 nM insulin stimulation for 30 minutes; surface-to-total insulin receptor assessed using cell surface biotinylation and Western blotting. Mouse strain background was not stated; ARF6 was not measured.

rows.Finding description: Primary Apoe−/− mouse neurons treated with apoE4 had lower cell surface insulin receptor abundance than neurons treated with apoE3, measured by cell surface biotinylation and Western blotting.
rows.Finding quote: As expected, cell surface IR was decreased after treatment with apoE4 compared with apoE3 (Figures S7A, B) without affecting the total IR (Figures S7A, G).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (lower cell surface insulin receptor abundance in primary Apoe−/− mouse neurons)
rows.Experimental system: Primary cortical neurons from embryonic day 16–18 Apoe−/− mice; glia depleted with Ara-C at DIV5. The cell surface biotinylation methods specify overnight treatment at DIV10 with 100 nM recombinant apoE, followed by surface biotinylation and Western blotting; the unavailable S7 legend prevents confirmation of panel-specific treatment details.

rows.Finding description: Surface-biotinylation Western blots of primary Apoe−/− mouse neurons treated with apoE4 versus apoE3 showed decreased surface insulin receptor (IR), with no significant difference in total IR or surface and total LRP1, NMDAR, AMPAR and Na-K-ATPase.
rows.Finding quote: As expected, cell surface IR was decreased after treatment with apoE4 compared with apoE3 (Figures S7A, B) without affecting the total IR (Figures S7A, G). No significant differences were found in the levels of cell surface and total LRP1, NMDAR, AMPAR, and Na-K-ATPase after apoE3 and apoE4 treatments (Figures S7A, C–F, H–K).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (decreased surface IR; no change in total IR or surface and total LRP1, NMDAR, AMPAR and Na-K-ATPase)
rows.Experimental system: Primary cortical neurons from embryonic day 16–18 Apoe−/− mice; cell-surface biotinylation methods specify treatment at DIV10 overnight with 100 nM recombinant apoE, followed by surface-protein isolation and Western blotting of surface and total proteins; panel-specific treatment details unavailable.

hypothesis: In some types of non-Alzheimer's, non-aged human brain cells, APOE4 adheres more tightly to some recycling receptors than APOE3, impeding recycling.

rows.Finding description: In six independent SPR experiments, lipid-free apoE4 bound purified human LRP1 more tightly than apoE3, with kinetic-model KD values of 202 ± 51 nM versus 456 ± 48 nM.
rows.Finding quote: Kinetic data from the best fit are summarized in Table 1 and reveal that the KD of apoE4 for LRP1 is 202 ± 51 nM, whereas apoE3 is 456 ± 48 nM and apoE2 is 529 ± 75 nM (Table 1).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (lower kinetic KD and higher affinity for LRP1)
rows.Experimental system: Cell-free SPR using a Biacore 3000; full-length human LRP1 purified from placenta and immobilized on a sensor chip; commercial recombinant lipid-free human apoE isoforms expressed in E. coli, injected at 52, 104, 208, 417, 834, and 1668 nM; association and dissociation globally fitted to a bivalent-binding model. Six independent experiments; no human brain cells, endosomal pH manipulation, or recycling assay.
rows.Data location: Fig 6 sensorgrams and model fits; Table 1 bKD column

rows.Finding description: Equilibrium analysis of the SPR experiments gave a lower LRP1 KD for lipid-free apoE4 than apoE3, with printed values of 236 ± 101 nM versus 398 ± 67 nM.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (lower equilibrium KD and higher affinity for LRP1)
rows.Experimental system: Cell-free Biacore 3000 SPR of commercial recombinant lipid-free human apoE expressed in E. coli binding immobilized full-length human LRP1 purified from placenta; equilibrium analysis of the apoE concentration series. The associated Fig 6 legend reports six independent experiments; receptor recycling was not assayed.
rows.Data location: Table 1 cKD column, ApoE3 and ApoE4 rows

rows.Finding description: Bivalent-model fitting gave apoE4 a numerically lower first dissociation rate constant from LRP1 than apoE3, with kd1 values of (6.5 ± 0.4) × 10−2 versus (9.0 ± 0.7) × 10−2 s−1; statistical significance was not reported.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (lower first dissociation rate constant from LRP1)
rows.Experimental system: Cell-free Biacore 3000 SPR; recombinant lipid-free human apoE expressed in E. coli and immobilized full-length human placental LRP1; global bivalent-model fitting of association and dissociation data. Six independent experiments reported in Fig 6 legend; endosomal dissociation and receptor recycling were not measured.
rows.Data location: Table 1 kd1 column, ApoE3 and ApoE4 rows

rows.Finding description: Bivalent-model fitting gave apoE4 a numerically higher first association rate constant for LRP1 than apoE3, with ka1 values of (6.2 ± 0.7) × 10^4 versus (4.3 ± 0.8) × 10^4 M−1 s−1; statistical significance was not reported.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (higher first association rate constant for LRP1)
rows.Experimental system: Cell-free Biacore 3000 SPR; recombinant lipid-free human apoE expressed in E. coli and immobilized full-length human placental LRP1; global bivalent-model fitting of association and dissociation data. Six independent experiments reported in Fig 6 legend; no receptor-recycling measurement.
rows.Data location: Table 1 ka1 column, ApoE3 and ApoE4 rows

rows.Finding description: Bivalent-model fitting gave apoE4 a slightly higher numerical second association rate constant than apoE3, with ka2 values of (9.9 ± 0.3) × 10−3 versus (9.6 ± 0.1) × 10−3 s−1; statistical significance was not reported.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (slightly higher second association rate constant in the LRP1 bivalent-binding model)
rows.Experimental system: Cell-free Biacore 3000 SPR; recombinant lipid-free human apoE expressed in E. coli binding immobilized full-length human placental LRP1; global bivalent-binding model. ka2 describes the model's second binding step. Six independent experiments reported in Fig 6 legend; no recycling assay.
rows.Data location: Table 1 ka2 column, ApoE3 and ApoE4 rows

rows.Finding description: Bivalent-model fitting gave apoE4 a slightly higher numerical second dissociation rate constant than apoE3, with kd2 values of (2.7 ± 0.3) × 10−3 versus (2.6 ± 0.2) × 10−3 s−1, opposing slower dissociation for this individual step; statistical significance was not reported.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (slightly higher second dissociation rate constant in the LRP1 bivalent-binding model)
rows.Experimental system: Cell-free Biacore 3000 SPR; recombinant lipid-free human apoE expressed in E. coli binding immobilized full-length human placental LRP1; global bivalent-binding model. kd2 describes dissociation from the model's bivalent complex. Six independent experiments reported in Fig 6 legend; endosomal pH-dependent dissociation and recycling were not assayed.
rows.Data location: Table 1 kd2 column, ApoE3 and ApoE4 rows

hypothesis: In some types of non-Alzheimer's, non-aged human brain cells, APOE4 undergoes increased aggregation in the endo-lysosome compared with APOE3.

rows.Finding description: Whole-cell fractionation immunoblots showed greater relative amounts of aggregated apoE in ApoE4 than ApoE3 primary mouse astrocytes, with three independent experiments reported for the associated quantification.
rows.Finding quote: The relative amount of aggregated ABCA1 and ApoE were significantly increased in ApoE4 primary astrocytes compared with ApoE3 primary astrocytes ( Fig. 4 D , E ).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (increased aggregated apoE in primary mouse astrocytes)
rows.Experimental system: Primary cortical astrocytes from 1–3-day-old mice homozygous for human APOE3 or APOE4 targeted replacement, backcrossed onto C57BL/6J for 10 generations; cultures approximately 95% astrocytes. Whole-cell lysates were separated into RIPA-soluble and RIPA-insoluble, guanidine-HCl-soluble fractions and immunoblotted for apoE. No endosomal or lysosomal localization of apoE aggregates was measured.

rows.Finding description: Hippocampal fractionation immunoblots showed greater relative amounts of aggregated apoE in male ApoE4-TR mice (n=8) than ApoE3-TR mice (n=6).
rows.Finding quote: In agreement, the relative amounts of aggregated ABCA1 and ApoE were greater in hippocampal homogenates of male ApoE4-TR mice ( n = 8) compared with ApoE3-TR mice ( n = 6) ( Fig. 4 F , G ).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (increased aggregated apoE in mouse hippocampus)
rows.Experimental system: Age-matched, 4-month-old male mice homozygous for human APOE3 or APOE4 targeted replacement on a C57BL/6J background. Hippocampal homogenates were separated into RIPA-soluble and guanidine-HCl-soluble fractions and immunoblotted for apoE; cell type and subcellular location of aggregates were not resolved.

rows.Finding description: Recombinant apoE4 formed numerically more aggregates than apoE3 after four hours at 37°C, but there was no significant difference (p=0.2); three independent experiments were reported for the associated quantification.
rows.Finding quote: rApoE4 protein formed more aggregates than rApoE3 protein when incubated ex vivo for 4 h at 37°C, although the observed increase in ApoE4 aggregation were not statistically significant ( p = 0.2; Fig. 4 H , I ).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (no change in recombinant apoE aggregation reaching statistical significance)
rows.Experimental system: Cell-free recombinant human apoE3 and apoE4, 10 μg each, incubated in RIPA buffer at 37°C for four hours; RIPA-soluble and guanidine-HCl-soluble fractions assessed by anti-apoE Western blot. This was neither an acidic-pH nor an endo-lysosomal experiment.

rows.Finding description: Quantification of three independent recombinant-protein experiments found no significant difference in aggregation between apoE4 and apoE3 after four hours at 37°C (p=0.2), despite a numerical increase for apoE4.
rows.Finding quote: rApoE4 protein formed more aggregates than rApoE3 protein when incubated ex vivo for 4 h at 37°C, although the observed increase in ApoE4 aggregation were not statistically significant ( p = 0.2; Fig. 4 H , I ).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (no change in recombinant apoE aggregation reaching statistical significance)
rows.Experimental system: Recombinant human apoE3 versus apoE4, 10 μg per preparation, incubated in RIPA buffer for four hours at 37°C; densitometric quantification of Western blots of RIPA-soluble and guanidine-HCl-soluble fractions. No cells, acidic-pH manipulation, or organelle localization.

rows.Finding description: CSF fractionation immunoblots from age- and sex-matched APOE ε4/ε4 carriers (n=5) and ε3/ε3 carriers (n=6) showed a 2.5-fold greater percentage of aggregated apoE in ε4/ε4 CSF.
rows.Finding quote: We then examined ApoE protein aggregation in human CSF from age and sex matched APOE ε3/ε3 ( n = 6) and ε4/ε4 ( n = 5) carriers. The results revealed greater percentage of aggregated ApoE protein in CSF of ε4/ε4 carriers (2.5-fold increased) compared with ε3/ε3 carriers ( Fig. 4 J , K ).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE ε3/ε3 -> APOE ε4/ε4) -> (increased aggregated apoE percentage in human CSF)
rows.Experimental system: Human CSF from six APOE ε3/ε3 and five APOE ε4/ε4 age- and sex-matched carriers; RIPA-soluble and guanidine-HCl-soluble apoE detected by Western blot, with Ponceau staining as loading control. This measures extracellular CSF apoE, without identifying its source cell or endo-lysosomal localization; ages are not supplied for this aggregation cohort.

hypothesis: In some types of non-Alzheimer's, non-aged human brain cells, APOE4 adheres more tightly to some recycling receptors than APOE3, impeding recycling.

rows.Finding description: SPR measurements showed high-affinity binding of lipid-free apoE3 and apoE4 to VLDLR without reported isoform discrimination; no significant difference was reported.
rows.Finding quote: Second, our experi- ments conﬁrmed that the VLDL receptor recognizes all apoE isoforms with equal afﬁnity.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (no change in lipid-free apoE binding affinity for VLDLR)
rows.Experimental system: Purified lipid-free apoE3 and apoE4 injected over immobilized soluble human VLDLR repeats 1–8 on CM5 SPR chips; receptor density 120 RU; HBS-P buffer, pH 7.4; 3-min binding at 25°C and 10 µl/min as specified in Fig 2; buffer replacement initiated dissociation; no brain cells or receptor recycling measured.

rows.Finding description: Purified VLDLR bound immobilized apoE3 and apoE4 without reported isoform discrimination—no significant difference was reported—with apparent Kd values of 59 and 77 nM, respectively, and two determinations per point.
rows.Finding quote: Thus, the results from this solid-phase assay suggest that both the VLDL receptor and LRP do not discriminate between apoE isoforms.
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (no change in VLDLR binding reported)
rows.Experimental system: Purified soluble human VLDLR ligand-binding repeats 1–8; purified apoE isoforms immobilized on microtiter wells at 4 µg/ml; increasing receptor concentrations incubated for 16 h at 4°C; antibody-based solid-phase binding assay and nonlinear regression; no brain cells or receptor-recycling measurement.
rows.Data location: Fig 1B–C; Results, Binding of apoE isoforms to LRP and the VLDL receptor

rows.Finding description: Immobilized LRP showed weak binding to lipid-free apoE4 but no detectable binding to lipid-free apoE3, although the authors suggested apoE4 aggregation might explain its weak interaction.
rows.Finding quote: In contrast, LRP failed to recognize lipid-free apoE2 and apoE3 and bound weakly to lipid-free apoE4 in solution (Fig. 2D–F).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (undetectable to weak lipid-free apoE binding to LRP)
rows.Experimental system: Purified lipid-free apoE isoforms and human placental LRP immobilized on CM5 SPR chips at 3,500 RU; apoE2/apoE3 disulfide-linked aggregates removed when present; HBS-P buffer, pH 7.4; 3-min binding at 25°C and 10 µl/min; no brain cells, endosomal conditions, or receptor recycling measured.
rows.Data location: Fig 2E–F; Results, The VLDL receptor recognizes lipid-free apoE isoforms

rows.Finding description: SPR detected no lipid-free apoE3 or apoE4 binding to LDLR, so no significant isoform difference was reported.
rows.Finding quote: As expected, the LDL receptor did not bind lipid-free apoE isoforms in SPR experiments (data not shown).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (no change in detectable lipid-free apoE binding to LDLR)
rows.Experimental system: Purified lipid-free apoE isoforms tested against soluble LDLR by SPR; soluble LDLR preparations were produced in Escherichia coli; LDLR-specific chip configuration and assay replication are not reported; no brain cells or receptor recycling measured.
rows.Data location: Table 1, LDL receptor row; Results, The VLDL receptor recognizes lipid-free apoE isoforms

hypothesis: In some types of non-Alzheimer's, non-aged human brain cells, for example astrocytes, APOE4 causes impaired ARF6-related recycling of receptors between the cell surface and the endosome, compared with APOE3.

rows.Finding description: In three independent experiments measuring surface and total GluN2B in Reelin-treated primary mouse cortical neurons, apoE4 reduced surface GluN2B more strongly than apoE3, and Slc9a6 deletion rescued the apoE4-induced reduction.
rows.Finding quote: Receptor surface levels show a stronger reduction with ApoE4 than ApoE3. NHE6 depletion counteracts the ApoE4-induced reduction of receptor surface expression. Cell surface biotinylation assay was performed for Apoer2 (C), GluN2B (D), GluA1, (E) and GluA2/3 (F).
rows.Finding summary: (apoE3 -> apoE4) -> (lower surface GluN2B in primary mouse neurons; rescued by Slc9a6 deletion)
rows.Experimental system: Primary cortical neurons from E18 wildtype and germline Slc9a6-knockout mouse littermates, including males and females; assayed at DIV10–14 after 30 min pretreatment with HEK293-derived human apoE3- or apoE4-conditioned medium (5 μg/ml), followed by Reelin (2 μg/ml) for an additional 30 min; surface GluN2B measured by cell-surface biotinylation and immunoblotting, and total GluN2B by whole-cell lysate immunoblotting with β-actin loading control; ARF6 was not measured.

rows.Finding description: In three independent experiments with primary embryonic mouse cortical neurons treated with Reelin, apoE4 reduced surface Apoer2 more strongly than apoE3, and Slc9a6 deletion restored surface expression, with recycling inferred from surface biotinylation and ARF6 not measured.
rows.Finding quote: Apoer2 recycling was completely restored in Slc9a6- neurons treated with ApoE4 (Figure 4C). We previously reported that the addition of ApoE3 to neurons also affects Apoer2 trafficking to a small, but reproducible extent. This was also abolished in Slc9a6- neurons (Figure 4C).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (lower surface Apoer2 in primary mouse cortical neurons; restored by Slc9a6 deletion)
rows.Experimental system: Primary cortical neurons from E18 Mus musculus embryos, comparing germline Slc9a6-null and wildtype littermates, including males and females; DIV10–14 cultures pretreated for 30 minutes with HEK293-derived human ApoE3- or ApoE4-conditioned medium (5 μg/ml), followed by Reelin (2 μg/ml) for another 30 minutes; surface Apoer2 measured by cell-surface biotinylation, NeutrAvidin capture, and immunoblotting, with total receptor levels assessed in whole-cell lysates.

hypothesis: In some types of non-Alzheimer's, non-aged human brain cells, APOE4 adheres more tightly to some recycling receptors than APOE3, impeding recycling.

rows.Finding description: Lipid-poor apoE4 bound isolated mouse brain microvessels less than apoE3, opposing greater overall apoE4 adhesion in this assay, although affinity and recycling were not measured.
rows.Finding quote: Lipid-poor apoE bound to the abluminal surfaces of isolated mouse brain microvessels in an isoform-specific manner, e.g., apoE2>apoE3>apoE4, and was almost displaced by excess unlabeled ligand (Figure 4 A).
rows.Finding summary: (lipid-poor apoE3 -> lipid-poor apoE4) -> (lower abluminal microvessel binding)
rows.Experimental system: Isolated mouse brain microvessels; general animal methods specify male C57BL/6-background mice aged 2–3 months; 2 nM radiolabeled Sf9-derived recombinant human lipid-poor apoE; binding at 4°C for 30 minutes, with or without 0.5 μM unlabeled ligand; inulin-corrected, TCA-precipitable binding.

rows.Finding description: Aβ40–apoE4 complexes lacked the LRP1 binding detected for Aβ40–apoE2 complexes while retaining VLDLR binding; this apoE2 comparison opposes stronger apoE4 interaction with LRP1.
rows.Finding quote: Aβ40-apoE2 and Aβ42-apoE2 complexes bound to both VLDLR and LRP1, whereas Aβ40-apoE4 and Aβ42-apoE4 complexes bound only to VLDLR, not to LRP1, as shown with the lipoprotein receptor–specific blocking antibodies (Figure 6 A).
rows.Finding summary: (Aβ40–apoE2 -> Aβ40–apoE4) -> (loss of detectable LRP1 binding)
rows.Experimental system: Isolated mouse brain microvessels; purified radiolabeled synthetic human Aβ40–human apoE complexes at 2 nM; binding at 4°C with receptor-blocking antibodies or 0.5 μM excess unlabeled ligand; Figure 6A does not specify lipidation state; n counts experiments per group.

hypothesis: In some types of non-Alzheimer's, non-aged human brain cells, APOE4 undergoes increased aggregation in the endo-lysosome compared with APOE3.

rows.Finding description: Cortical fractionation in mice at 3 and 22 months, with 4–6 mice/genotype, showed an increased insoluble-to-soluble apoE ratio with aging in APOE4 mice and a smaller upward trend in APOE3 mice, without identifying the aggregates' cellular compartment.
rows.Finding quote: Intriguingly, the level of insoluble apoE was significantly increased in aged apoE4-TR mice compared with that in young mice (Figure 7E), leading to an increased insoluble to soluble ratio of apoE with aging (Figure 7F). To a lesser extent, there was a trend of an increased insoluble to soluble apoE ratio with aging in apoE3-TR mice (Figures 7E, F).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (more pronounced age-associated increase in the cortical insoluble-to-soluble apoE ratio)
rows.Experimental system: Human APOE3- or APOE4-targeted-replacement mice, with the endogenous murine Apoe locus replaced by human APOE; mixed sexes, 3 and 22 months old; cortical RIPA-soluble and guanidine-extracted detergent-insoluble apoE quantified by ELISA and used to calculate the insoluble-to-soluble ratio; no AD model or endosome/lysosome localization reported.

hypothesis: In some types of non-Alzheimer's, non-aged human brain cells, APOE4 adheres more tightly to some recycling receptors than APOE3, impeding recycling.

rows.Finding description: Normalized transferrin recycling rates showed no significant difference reported between APOE4 and APOE3 cells; the paper describes the rates as similar, with six independent differentiations for pair 1 and three for pair 2.
rows.Finding quote: Similarly, the total amount of Tf after a 20-min pulse was higher in ApoE4 compared to ApoE3 iCE-BECs (Figure 6B), but the recycling rate was similar between the two genetic variants (Figure 6D).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (no change in normalized transferrin recycling rate)
rows.Experimental system: Human homozygous isogenic BIONi037-A/APOE3 versus BIONi037-A4/APOE4 and Alstem iPS26/APOE3 versus iPS16/APOE4 iCE-BECs on differentiation day 14. A 20-minute pulse of 25 micrograms/mL fluorescent transferrin followed by a 0–60-minute chase with 250 micrograms/mL unlabeled holo-transferrin. Retained fluorescence was normalized to each condition’s immediate-post-pulse value and fitted exponentially. This measures transferrin clearance as a surrogate for TfR1 recycling, not apoE-bound receptor recycling.
